newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan blast set off 200 tonnes of explosives -sources.
newsitem.headline: Afghan blast set off 200 tonnes of explosives -sources.

text.p: About 200 tonnes of explosives may have been detonated in the massive accidental blast at an ammunition dump in the eastern city of Jalalabad, in which at least 30 people died, U.N. sources said on Thursday.

A Pakistan-based Afghan news service had said in its first report about 40 people were killed by Wednesday's explosion which flattened the Islamic Taleban militia's security department headquarters, and residents said the toll could be more than 100, including local police chief Mullah Abdul Ahad.

But the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Assistance to Afghanistan (UNOCHA), quoted an assessment team report as putting the casualties at 30 dead and 191 injured, at least 80 of them seriously.
"The team estimates that the volume of explosives that was detonated could be as much as 200 tonnes," said a UNOCHA statement issued in neighbouring Pakistan.
"This ranks as one of the biggest accidental munitions explosions ever," it quoted Ian Bullpint, a UNOCHA mines clearance official, as saying.
"Most explosions of this kind have occurred in military installations located some way from residential areas," he added. "The tragedy here is that so many civilians have been affected."
Residents said more than 30 civilians had died in one house.
On Thursday, old men dug through rubble to salvage belongings from their shattered homes.
The explosion ripped a crater 50 metres (yards) wide by 10 metres deep in the compound in a western city district.
No walls were left standing and only a 3.5-metre high pile of rubble indicated where the main building had been.
Taleban fighters tried to keep people away from the scene, littered with half-buried mortars and rockets, but no particular security alert appeared to be in force in the city.

The blast, which UNOCHA said was the fourth major munitions store explosion in Afghanistan in recent years, scattered ammunition and explosives over a radius of about 1.5 km (one mile), demolishing several houses near the security department and damaging scores more.
Last year, ordnance exploded in the southern city of Kandahar and the capital Kabul.
"I think it was possibly between 100 and 200 tonnes (of explosives)," Noel Spencer, head of the U.N. mine clearing technical department, told Reuters at the scene.

UNOCHA said it was sending six teams of explosives experts to clear the area of unexploded munitions and debris. The World Food Programme has provided the regional hospital in Jalalabad, with more than 13 tonnes of food and the World Health Organisation has donated about a tonne of medical emergency supplies.

Pakistani newspapers quoted Mullah Sadr-i-Azam, deputy governor of Nangarhar province, of which Jalalabad is the capital, as saying the accidental explosion of an artillery shell had set off the blast at the arms depot.
He denied the possibility of sabotage and said four Taleban guards and six civilians had died in the blast.
The Taleban, fired by zeal to spread their strict version of Islam across Afghanistan, captured Jalalabad in September from a group of neutral guerrilla factions before marching on to Kabul.
